lessons.name: LeRobot community (Hugging Face)
lessons.summary: The LeRobot community is the open group of developers, students, and labs who build, test, and share data for Hugging Face's LeRobot library.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

The LeRobot community is the open group of developers, students, and labs who build, test, and share data for Hugging Face's LeRobot library.

![Participants of the LeRobot hackathon hub at 42 Paris, June 2025](/img/lessons/orgs_other-lerobot-community.webp)
*Participants at 42 Paris, June 2025. Source: [42AI hackathon highlights](https://42-ai.github.io/posts/LeRobotHackathonHighlights/), CC BY 4.0, Mathieu Perez.*

## What they do in robotics

- **Shared workflow:** teleoperate means control the robot yourself; record demonstrations, train a policy (the learned controller), then deploy it on the robot.
- **Open code:** `huggingface/lerobot` uses Apache-2.0 and welcomes code, documentation, datasets, and hardware integrations.
- **Shared datasets:** members publish robot demonstrations on the Hugging Face Hub, much like publishing packages to npm.
- **Worldwide hackathon:** June 14–15, 2025 combined online participation and local hubs; submissions included a short demo video and datasets where relevant.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Teleoperate] --> B[Record data] --> C[Train policy] --> D[Deploy]
```

> **Key idea:** Sharing demonstrations lets another team inspect and reuse the data behind a robot experiment.

## Why they matter for 42AI

- **Local experience:** 42AI's recap reports four 42 Paris teams in the top 30, including LeChef first and LeSplat third.
- **Concrete starting task:** the real-world tutorial records picking up a Lego block and placing it in a bin with an SO-101.
- **Map connection:** “Assemble & teleoperate an SO-101” prepares the hardware for that learning workflow.

## How to engage

1. **Watch the hackathon demos** to see what teams built.
2. **Follow the real-world tutorial** before modifying the workflow; use the docs' Discord link for help.
3. **Publish a documented dataset** describing the task and recording setup.
4. **Contribute a focused fix** using the contribution guide's issue and pull-request templates.

lessons.name: Open Source Robotics Foundation (Open Robotics)
lessons.summary: Open Robotics, the Open Source Robotics Foundation, is the nonprofit that stewards ROS, Gazebo, and related open-source robot software.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Open Robotics, the Open Source Robotics Foundation, is the nonprofit that stewards ROS, Gazebo, and related open-source robot software.

![A simple mobile manipulator robot with gripper, sensor, and wheels in the Gazebo simulator](/img/lessons/orgs_other-open-robotics.webp)
*A robot in Gazebo 7, a historical simulator release. Source: [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Gazebo_7_Simple_mobile_manipulator.png), Apache License 2.0, Jose Luis Rivero.*

## What they do in robotics

- **Shared tools:** ROS provides robot software libraries; Gazebo simulates robots; ros-controls connects control software to hardware; Open-RMF coordinates fleets and building infrastructure.
- **Shared infrastructure:** build servers and continuous integration automatically compile and check these projects.
- **Community governance:** the Open Source Robotics Alliance (OSRA), launched in 2024, organizes technical decisions and funding under the foundation's oversight.

Think of a language foundation maintaining the runtime and package infrastructure: applications depend on shared tools that need care beyond one team's project.

> **Key idea:** Maintaining the tools, infrastructure, and decision process is part of keeping robot applications usable over time.

## Why they matter for 42AI

- **Practical example:** use ROS 2 to structure a robot application and Gazebo to test it in a simulated world before hardware trials.
- **Meet other users:** ROSCon Global is a developer conference; its announced 2027 edition is October 12–14 in Kraków.
- **Separate organizations:** Intrinsic acquired the commercial subsidiaries' business in December 2022; the nonprofit foundation continues under the Open Robotics brand.

## How to engage

1. **Watch the project-update keynote** for examples of ROS 2 and Gazebo development.
2. **Read the OSRA announcement** to understand how contributors participate in project decisions.
3. **Choose one project** and reproduce a small issue before proposing a fix.

lessons.name: OROCA
lessons.summary: OROCA is a Korean community for open-source robotics software and hardware, connecting an online forum, local groups, and public GitHub projects.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

OROCA is a Korean community for open-source robotics software and hardware, connecting an online forum, local groups, and public GitHub projects.

![Assembly photo in OROCA's iTurtle project repository](/img/lessons/orgs_other-oroca.webp)
*Assembly photo published with iTurtle. Source: [OROCA image file](https://github.com/oroca/iTurtle/blob/master/img/SeoulHardwareHackathon_263.JPG), Apache License 2.0 (repository license), photographer unknown.*

## What they do in robotics

- **Learning forum:** the Naver cafe opened on December 25, 2012; its boards cover ROS, microcontrollers (small computers for electronics), and local meetups.
- **Robot projects:** iTurtle is a miniature TurtleBot3-based project from OROCA's Pangyo group; the organization also publishes OROCA-EduBot and ROS teaching packages.
- **Seminar recordings:** OROCA's channel includes an Open Robotics Seminar talk about game engines and ROS 2 simulation.

It works like a regional Stack Overflow plus a makers' meetup: questions, shared code, and physical builds support each other.

> **Key idea:** A shared robot project gives a learning community something concrete to inspect, improve, and discuss.

## Why they matter for 42AI

- **Community example:** 42AI could combine short talks, a question board, and a shared robot design in Paris.
- **Concrete contribution:** iTurtle's README invites documentation corrections, improvement ideas, issues, and pull requests.
- **Historical examples:** the linked ROS tutorials include an Indigo cheatsheet; they illustrate older ROS workflows rather than a current ROS 2 installation.

## How to engage

1. **Watch the seminar recording**, using translation if needed; the talk and forum are in Korean.
2. **Inspect the iTurtle repository** and compare its design with the related TurtleBot3 map node.
3. **Read the forum's public boards** and check repository activity before proposing a small documentation fix.

lessons.name: Poppy Project
lessons.summary: Poppy Project is an open-source, 3D-printed robot platform, born in 2012 at Inria's Flowers lab, for research, education, and art.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Poppy Project is an open-source, 3D-printed robot platform, born in 2012 at Inria's Flowers lab, for research, education, and art.

![An open-source, 3D-printed Poppy humanoid robot](/img/lessons/orgs_other-poppy-project.webp)
*Poppy Humanoid. Source: [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Open-Source_3D_printed_Poppy_humanoid_robot.jpg), CC BY-SA 4.0, Inria / Poppy-project.org / Photo H. Raguet.*

## What they do in robotics

- **Open designs:** Poppy Humanoid and Poppy Ergo Jr share printable parts, assembly information, and software; Poppy Torso is another supported robot shape.
- **Small-arm example:** Poppy Ergo Jr has six movable joints, Dynamixel XL-320 motors, and Raspberry Pi control, with lampshade, grasper, or pen-holder tools.
- **Motor software:** pypot is a Python library for controlling supported Dynamixel motors; its README lists compatible models, including XL-320.
- **Reuse rules:** the robot repositories distinguish Creative Commons BY-SA hardware from GPL v3 software; the Poppy name is a protected trademark.

Think of an open-source app whose repository also includes the files for manufacturing its enclosure and assembling its components.

> **Key idea:** Sharing a robot means documenting the physical parts and their assembly as well as publishing code.

## Why they matter for 42AI

- **French example:** the project originated in Inria Bordeaux Sud-Ouest's Flowers laboratory.
- **Design exercise:** trace the Ergo Jr's six joints through its parts list, printable shapes, and software before considering a build.
- **Check the assumptions:** the Ergo Jr README describes Raspberry Pi 2/3 setup; its compatibility with a new setup needs verification.

## How to engage

1. **Watch the humanoid overview** to connect the printed structure with the moving robot.
2. **Inspect the Ergo Jr hardware folder** and bill of materials (the list of required parts).
3. **Read pypot's compatibility list** before choosing motors; check repository activity and existing issues before contributing.

lessons.name: PX4 open-source community
lessons.summary: The PX4 community is a global group of developers and companies building open-source flight-control software for drones and other unmanned vehicles.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

The PX4 community is a global group of developers and companies building open-source flight-control software for drones and other unmanned vehicles.

![A Pixhawk flight controller board, the open hardware PX4 often runs on](/img/lessons/orgs_other-px4.webp)
*A Pixhawk flight controller. Source: [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pixhawk.png), CC BY 4.0, Pixhawk project authors.*

## What they do in robotics

- **Autopilot software:** PX4 controls vehicles such as drones and rovers; an autopilot reads sensors and calculates commands for motors and other moving parts.
- **Neutral support:** the Dronecode Foundation supports the PX4 ecosystem; its community includes independent developers and companies.
- **Shared development:** Dronecode's 2025 review reports 651 contributors from 99 organizations across its projects, including PX4, QGroundControl, MAVLink, and MAVSDK.
- **Release example:** that review describes PX4 v1.16's redesigned rover support and improved ROS 2 integration.

An autopilot is like a continuously running service: read incoming sensor data, update the vehicle's estimated state, and produce control outputs.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Sensor readings] --> B[Estimate state] --> C[Calculate commands] --> D[Vehicle motion] --> A
```

> **Key idea:** A shared flight stack lets teams focus on an application while reusing the community's vehicle-control software.

## Why they matter for 42AI

- **Hardware-free example:** PX4's software-in-the-loop simulation runs the flight software on a computer connected to a simulated vehicle.
- **Shared tools:** Gazebo and ROS 2 connect aerial experiments with tools used elsewhere in the lab.

## How to engage

1. **Watch the platform overview**, then follow the current development setup docs rather than copying an old video's commands.
2. **Try a simulated vehicle** using the simulation guide before considering hardware.
3. **Join Discord or the weekly developer call**, which the community page lists as open to interested developers.
4. **Report a reproducible issue** with logs through the project's public tracker.

lessons.name: ROS Japan Users Group
lessons.summary: The ROS Japan Users Group (ROS Japan UG) is a volunteer community that runs ROS study sessions, talk nights, and hackathons in Japan.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

The ROS Japan Users Group (ROS Japan UG) is a volunteer community that runs ROS study sessions, talk nights, and hackathons in Japan.

![People attending ROS Japan UG's ROSCon and iREX recap meeting](/img/lessons/orgs_other-ros-japan-ug.webp)
*Photo on the group's December 2025 recap event page. Source: [ROS Japan UG #60](https://rosjp.connpass.com/event/376159/), license unknown, photographer unknown.*

## What they do in robotics

- **Peer learning:** ROS is a robot software framework; this group helps people learn and use it through meetings, workshops, and shared materials.
- **Short talks:** event #60 used ten-minute presentations to share ROSCon experiences, simulation topics, and other practical lessons.
- **Hands-on events:** #62 explored Kachaka robot development through AI-assisted coding; its public repository shares supporting ROS 2 materials.
- **Public channels:** Connpass lists events and recordings, GitHub hosts materials, and the group advertises a move from Slack to Open Robotics' Zulip chat.

Think of a local Python meetup: a large software ecosystem becomes easier to enter when someone demonstrates one small problem and answers questions.

> **Key idea:** Short demonstrations and shared materials let a user group turn individual debugging experience into community knowledge.

## Why they matter for 42AI

- **Repeatable format:** try a ten-minute explanation of one ROS 2 problem, followed by questions and a published example.
- **Welcoming entry point:** Connpass explicitly welcomes beginners; the #60 event included places for students and first-time participants.
- **Language context:** the linked meeting recordings and event descriptions are in Japanese.

## How to engage

1. **Watch a recorded talk night** to see how presenters explain their work.
2. **Browse the event materials** and compare one example with your own ROS 2 setup.
3. **Join the group through Connpass**, then follow its current Japan-channel link to Zulip for discussion.

lessons.name: ROS-Industrial Consortium Europe
lessons.summary: ROS-Industrial Consortium Europe (RIC-EU) is the European branch of ROS-Industrial, led by Fraunhofer IPA in Stuttgart, helping factories adopt ROS 2.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

ROS-Industrial Consortium Europe (RIC-EU) is the European branch of ROS-Industrial, led by Fraunhofer IPA in Stuttgart, helping factories adopt ROS 2.

![A talk at the ROS-Industrial Europe Conference 2025 in Strasbourg](/img/lessons/orgs_other-ric-europe.webp)
*ROS-Industrial Europe Conference 2025. Source: [ROS-Industrial recap](https://rosindustrial.org/news/2026/2/17/ros-2-in-industry-key-takeaways-from-the-ros-industrial-conference-2025), license unknown.*

## What they do in robotics

- **Member consortium:** a consortium is a group of organizations working together; RIC-EU offers technical support, training, and joint open-source development projects.
- **European lead:** Fraunhofer IPA leads RIC-EU; separate research-led consortia coordinate work in North America and Asia-Pacific.
- **Factory experience:** the 13th European conference ran in Strasbourg on November 17–18, 2025, covering robot drivers, real-time control, and humanoid safety.
- **Concrete software need:** a driver connects an application to hardware; conference talks explain what industrial ROS 2 users need from those connections.

Think of an industry working group for an open-source framework: users pool effort on shared problems instead of each company rebuilding the same components.

> **Key idea:** Factory software needs predictable timing and maintainable interfaces as well as a working robot demo.

## Why they matter for 42AI

- **Learn requirements:** the conference recap explains practical deployment challenges, including long-term maintenance.
- **Meet practitioners:** the announced 2026 conference is December 3–4 at Fraunhofer IPA, with lab tours.
- **Prepare a useful question:** compare a small ROS 2 demo with a conference case study and identify one missing production requirement.

## How to engage

1. **Watch the EU consortium update** for an introduction from the organizers.
2. **Read the 2025 recap**, then choose one technical talk to study.
3. **Use the EU page's newsletter and event links** to find public opportunities; check each event's access and registration details.

lessons.name: Webots open-source community
lessons.summary: The Webots open-source community is the group of users and contributors around Webots, a free robot simulator released as open source in December 2018.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

The Webots open-source community is the group of users and contributors around Webots, a free robot simulator released as open source in December 2018.

![The Webots interface with a simulated car, scene tree, and code editor](/img/lessons/orgs_other-webots.webp)
*A historical Webots interface screenshot. Source: [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Wbinterface.png), CC BY-SA 4.0, DavidMansolino.*

## What they do in robotics

- **Shared simulator:** Webots models and simulates robots and their surroundings; Cyberbotics develops it with contributions from users.
- **Familiar languages:** a controller is the program defining a robot's behavior; the first tutorial includes C, C++, Python, Java, and MATLAB examples.
- **Open collaboration:** the Apache-2.0 repository provides code, issues, Discussions, and contribution instructions.
- **Many contribution types:** the guide welcomes bug reports, documentation, Python examples, translations, and robot models.

Think of a simulator as a test environment with a visible world: your controller program sends commands to virtual motors instead of a physical machine.

> **Key idea:** A small, reproducible simulated world gives other contributors a practical way to understand and debug your robot code.

## Why they matter for 42AI

- **First exercise:** Tutorial 1, labelled 30 minutes, creates an arena, adds an e-puck robot, and programs its wheels.
- **Software-first start:** teams can inspect code and behavior together before choosing hardware.
- **Community versus service:** public Discussions support user questions; Cyberbotics also offers paid training, consulting, and support.

## How to engage

1. **Follow Tutorial 1** and save the world and controller together.
2. **Ask a focused question** in Discussions, including enough information to reproduce the problem.
3. **Choose a beginner issue or documentation fix** using the contributing guide; attach the small simulation when reporting a bug.
